source_neutral.procedure: Examine delay observations for one approval workflow, with named case types and a fixed time window, handoff by handoff. Define each handoff interval as the time from completion of the upstream step to the downstream approver's first action, separate from the approver's working time. Apply the process where elapsed time at a handoff plausibly has more than one explanation. Generate candidate mechanisms, specify their predictions, gather evidence that distinguishes among them, and update a ranked set for each handoff. Multiple mechanisms may coexist at a handoff. Before use, verify that ticket histories contain stage-level timestamps, reassignment and return events are logged, and staffing schedules and queue lengths can be aligned to the scoped window.
source_neutral.action:
1. Fix the workflow, case types and observation window. Define the handoff interval and check whether timestamps represent the events they are assumed to represent, testing measurement artifact first.
2. Before examining evidence that distinguishes among mechanisms, list candidates for each handoff, including a residual category for mechanisms not yet identified. Assign rough initial likelihoods based on each mechanism's frequency for this kind of team and case mix. Record who proposed each candidate and why.
3. For every candidate, state predicted and contradicting patterns in advance. Select checks for which candidates predict different results: compare wait time with arrivals per staffed hour to distinguish capacity shortfall from batching or fixed cadence; examine release clustering by clock time or weekday for fixed cadence; examine delay concentrated in returned or reopened tickets for submission defects; examine long time to first assignment and repeated reassignment for unclear ownership or misrouting; examine arrival-to-first-open gaps that shorten after reminders for notification or visibility failure; examine pending-on-third-party status for external dependencies; compare delay with competing workload peaks versus approval volume for priority displacement; examine concentration of delay on specific approvers' absence dates for single-approver dependence; and examine delay confined to case types with mandated review for policy- or risk-required holds or sequential review.
4. Gather evidence according to its ability to distinguish candidates and its cost: existing ticket histories first, then queue lengths and staffing schedules, then exception-case inspection, then interviews. Use interviews to generate candidates and mechanism detail; do not treat them as independent confirmation of patterns already suggested by logs.
5. After every evidence item, update the handoff-by-candidate matrix with supports, contradicts or does not discriminate, and re-rank candidates. Add candidates raised by exception cases or interviews.
6. Retain single-approver dependence and required holds or sequential review until specifically contradicted, even at low rank, because ignoring dependence on one approver or bypassing a required hold carries high cost.
7. Apply the stopping conditions separately to each handoff. If none holds, retain several candidates and continue gathering evidence. Do not assert a single cause to close the analysis.
source_neutral.observables: Track how each evidence item changes the handoff-by-candidate matrix: which candidates it supports, contradicts or leaves undifferentiated. Inputs include the distribution of handoff intervals by stage and case type; wait time relative to arrivals per staffed hour; approval release clustering by clock time or weekday; the share of delay associated with return, reopen or reassignment events; time from arrival to first assignment and first open; changes in arrival-to-first-open gaps after reminders; overlap of long waits with specific approvers' absences or competing workload peaks; pending-on-external status and its duration; concentration of delay in case types with mandated review; discrepancies between logged timestamps and other traces of the same event; and interview accounts and exception-case details. Record a check whose result is predicted equally by every candidate as non-discriminating, rather than supporting the candidates. During a pilot, observe whether turnaround at the targeted handoff moves in the pre-declared direction under comparable demand and staffing, and whether delay reappears at an adjacent handoff.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Evidence patterns justify re-ranking, eliminating or retaining candidate mechanisms at each handoff. The result is a narrowed, ranked set, without asserting a single cause. Identify where delay accumulates by reporting the handoffs with the largest intervals, their retained mechanisms, and evidence for and against those mechanisms. Identify potentially useful bounded changes by matching changes to retained mechanisms and prioritising changes that several retained candidates call for. Eliminate a candidate only when a check capable of detecting it produces a contradicting observation. Lack of support from a weak check leaves the candidate retained at lower rank. Timestamp and queue patterns support statements about association and location. Interviews support additional candidates and mechanism detail. A pilot response in the declared direction raises the targeted mechanism's rank for that handoff and supports assessment of the bounded change. A non-response lowers its rank and returns the handoff to consideration of alternative mechanisms. Coexisting mechanisms are an allowed conclusion.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: Use handoffs within the scoped workflow as the units of analysis, with a matrix relating each handoff to its candidate mechanisms. Keep handoff waiting intervals separate from approver working time. The proposed starting candidates are possibilities to investigate, not established facts: (a) capacity shortfall, where arrivals exceed staffed approver time; (b) batching or fixed review cadence, where items wait for scheduled review; (c) incomplete or defective submissions that are returned and re-enter the queue; (d) unclear ownership or misrouting, where items remain unassigned or are reassigned; (e) notification or visibility failure, where the approver is unaware an item is waiting; (f) an external dependency or missing information; (g) priority displacement by competing work; (h) dependence on one approver who is absent without a delegate; (i) a deliberate hold or sequential review required by policy or risk; (j) measurement artifact from logged timestamps lagging real events; and (k) a residual category for mechanisms not yet listed. More than one mechanism may operate at a handoff. Mechanisms can interact through shared staff and queues, and reducing delay at one handoff can shift it to another.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: Pilot one bounded change matched to the leading candidate at a handoff. Specified examples are a delegate rule for single-approver dependence, a submission checklist for incomplete or defective submissions, an explicit owner and alert for unclear ownership or notification failure, and a changed review cadence for batching or fixed cadence. Declare the expected response before the pilot and compare turnaround under comparable demand and staffing. Check whether delay reappears at an adjacent handoff. If the expected response does not occur, reopen consideration of candidate mechanisms for that handoff instead of escalating the same change. Generalising beyond the scoped workflow, case types and window requires rechecking under comparable demand and staffing.
source_neutral.limits:
Stop gathering evidence for a handoff when any one of these conditions holds: all remaining candidates call for the same bounded change; the remaining available checks do not distinguish among retained candidates; or all but one or two candidates have been contradicted by at least two sources that do not share an origin. If none holds, keep several candidates open and continue. Do not declare a single cause to close the analysis.
Coverage depends on the generated candidate list. A mechanism never generated cannot be ranked; the residual category flags that possibility without identifying it.
Timestamps may be incomplete or lag real events. Logs from one ticketing system share its errors. Interviewees may repeat dashboard information, so agreement between logs and interviews may not provide independent corroboration.
The checks have no measured sensitivity or specificity in this setting. Return flags can miss informal rework outside the ticketing system. A relationship between load and waiting time can arise from both capacity shortfall and priority displacement.
Bias can arise from accepting the first-named location of delay or the account of the most senior or vocal interviewee, closing the analysis when one handoff appears worst, giving a vivid exception more weight than the common pattern, or selecting tickets to confirm an existing explanation. Pre-stated predictions and retention of the residual category reduce these biases without removing them.
The data are observational. Case mix, staffing and demand can confound comparisons. Pilot changes can reflect regression to the mean, attention effects or concurrent changes. A response in the expected direction does not prove the mechanism, and relieving one handoff can shift delay to another.
The procedure narrows explanations; it does not quantify hidden stage contributions or estimate system dynamics. Conclusions are bounded by the scoped workflow, case types and time window. Mechanisms interact through shared staff and queues. This reasoning procedure is not a validated protocol for the approval-workflow setting.
